items.stem: Per the attribution principle — a metric mover must be traceable to a segment — a weekly dashboard reports only overall accuracy holding flat. Logs carry no regulated or personal data, but one high-volume segment is suspected of failing beneath that trend. What should the team add?

opts.t: Reconfigure alerting to trigger on segment-level rates rather than on every individual error.
Expand stratified sampling of the high-confidence automated stream feeding the quality grading pipeline.
Redact identifying fields at write time, set a retention window, and restrict dashboard access.
Add per-segment breakdowns to the dashboard so each segment's trend is visible independently.

items.whyRight: The dashboard's defect is that it reports only an aggregate, exactly the masking pattern this section warns against: a flat overall number can conceal a segment failing well below bar. Per-segment breakdowns are the only option that restores segment-level visibility to the report itself.

whyWrong.A: Alerting cadence is a different control than dashboard reporting; the stem describes a reporting gap, not events firing individually, so this targets the wrong layer.
whyWrong.B: The stated gap is reporting granularity on an already-produced number, not which cases enter the grading pipeline; expanding sampling coverage doesn't add a segment view.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the logs carry no regulated or personal data, so redaction and retention controls address a risk this scenario never raises.

items.t1Clause: Logs carry no regulated or personal data

items.stem: A financial-services team is replacing a manual claims-review process that a compliance director confirms currently runs at a measured 8% error rate across 40,000 claims processed monthly. Before launch, how should the new system's pass bar for that error rate be set?

opts.t: Defer setting the bar until the new system's own baseline scores are available, then calibrate against them.
Set the bar at 0 per N, since this is treated as a deterministic property.
Re-anchor the bar to a small non-zero rate such as 0.1%, since zero is unreachable.
Set the new system's pass bar to beat the manual process's measured 8% error rate.

items.whyRight: The process being replaced already has a measured real-world error rate, which is the strongest available anchor for a bar. The replacement's pass bar should be tied to and required to beat that 8%, not set independently of the process it succeeds.

whyWrong.A: Setting the bar only after the new system's own results are in describes what happened rather than gating the decision; the 8% baseline was available before launch.
whyWrong.B: Zero per N applies to a deterministic property like a forbidden PII field, not a statistical error rate on a process already measured at 8%.
whyWrong.C: An arbitrary small rate discards the process's own measured 8% baseline, which is a stronger and more relevant anchor than an unrelated placeholder figure.

items.t1Clause: currently runs at a measured 8% error rate

items.stem: A legal-research assistant cites statute sections in every answer; compliance counsel needs proof each citation is drawn precisely from the statute text, not merely phrased in a formal register, before a filing deadline. Which instrument should validate each citation?

opts.t: Score citations against a detailed grading rubric using a model judge.
Run a deterministic check that each cited span exists verbatim in the source document.
Compute a lexical overlap score between each citation and its claimed source passage.
Route a sample of cited outputs to human reviewers for spot-checking.

items.whyRight: Citation validity is exact and machine-decidable: either the string appears verbatim in the source document or it does not. A deterministic check settles it precisely and for free, where a model judge has been measured at roughly chance-level accuracy on this property.

whyWrong.A: A rubric-scored model judge introduces grader error into a property code can settle exactly; judges have been measured at roughly chance on citation validity.
whyWrong.C: A lexical overlap score is a similarity measure, not an existence check; a citation can score high on overlap while never appearing verbatim in the source.
whyWrong.D: Human review is the calibration instrument for this section, not the scaling one; spending it on an exact check the code already settles wastes the scarcest resource.

items.t1Clause: not merely phrased in a formal register

items.stem: A controlled A/B test on a new prompt variant, with model and retrieval depth unchanged, runs its full declared 14-day duration. The primary quality metric improves 2 points, but p95 latency crosses the pre-declared guardrail. What should the team do?

opts.t: Split the change into separate prompt, model, and retrieval-depth variants so the improvement can be attributed to one cause.
Roll out to a limited percentage of traffic while continuing to monitor the latency guardrail for further breaches.
Do not ship the variant; the declared latency guardrail was breached regardless of the quality gain.
Extend the test for another 14 days to confirm whether the latency breach persists.

items.whyRight: Guardrails are declared before launch specifically so they can block a launch regardless of how much the primary metric improved. The variant crossed its pre-declared latency guardrail, so the correct action is to withhold shipping even though quality gained ground.

whyWrong.A: The stem states model and retrieval depth never changed; only the prompt did, so there is already one clean variable, and splitting variants that didn't move solves nothing here.
whyWrong.B: Monitoring after a partial launch is a detective posture; the guardrail was declared as a preventive gate, and a confirmed breach should block launch outright.
whyWrong.D: The declared 14-day duration has already run; the guardrail breach is already known, and extending the test only delays a decision the data already supports.

items.t1Clause: p95 latency crosses the pre-declared guardrail

items.stem: A customer-support assistant retrieves the correct policy passages and states accurate facts, but omits the numbered remediation steps compliance mandates. Retrieval Recall@k is verified at target and the facts check out. What is the most likely fix layer?

opts.t: Escalate to a higher-capability model to produce more thorough, complete responses.
Re-index the corpus and re-verify retrieval chunk boundaries.
Add explicit formatting instructions specifying the required steps to the system prompt.
Add few-shot examples demonstrating the required response format.

items.whyRight: The facts are accurate and retrieval already clears its bar, which rules out the data and retrieval layer entirely. The missing element is a required output structure, which this order of diagnosis assigns to the prompt and instruction layer, not to the model.

whyWrong.A: Retrieval is already verified and the facts are correct, so nothing implicates the model; escalating discards a component that was never shown to be at fault.
whyWrong.B: The stem already states Recall@k is verified at target, so the retrieval layer is cleared; re-indexing targets a layer the evidence has already ruled out.
whyWrong.D: Few-shot examples fix formatting that stays inconsistent despite explicit instructions; here the steps are missing outright, so a plain instruction fix comes first.

items.t1Clause: Retrieval Recall@k is verified at target and the facts check out

notes: g40: shape S3 applied to a release-gating decision (A/B guardrail breach) rather than a classic root-cause diagnosis, following the same reading already used for F-4.9-02 elsewhere in this paper's shape assignments — the 'pin what didn't change, order the decision' mechanic carries over cleanly but flagging the interpretation for the grounding audit.

g41: shape S4 applied to the diagnosis-order table in 4.10 by treating the symptom's shape (facts correct, steps missing, retrieval already cleared) as the 'stated shape' and the four fix layers as the competing mechanisms — consistent with S4's definition but noting the mapping since 4.10 isn't one of the shape's example sections in ARCHETYPE-LEDGER.md.
